utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as they go to get the witness, I would note for the record that the Prosecution had intended, that as part of this witness' evidence, we would provide the prior testimony of this witness in the Tadic case. We know that last evening, yesterday afternoon, we spoke about the question regarding the admissibility of prior statements. We would ask the Court if a decision has been made at least as regards prior testimony of a witness so that we know whether we should tender that or whether we should proceed without the prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet, Ms. Hollis. We haven't decided yet. We're trying to expedite the process and have a ruling by the Trial Chamber, because it is a priority, of course, but we haven't taken a final ruling with regard to prior testimony yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Defence have any objections to having the Tadic transcript tendered and that testimony, the prior testimony? It is the transcript, not the prior testimony, but the Tadic transcript. Mr. Simic, do you have a response from your collective?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This has taken us by surprise so we haven't had a chance to confer, and I'll be speaking in my name. We opened that question yesterday; we started the question. Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan presented our views on behalf of Mr. Kos and Kvocka, and we don't want to violate our principle before we get a ruling, and I speak for Mr. Kvocka's Defence, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. O'Sullivan. We are talking about a transcript, not about prior testimony. Yesterday we were speaking about prior testimony of witnesses. Now we're speaking about the LiveNote, the transcript of the Tadic audience. I think that that perhaps changes matters somewhat. That is what we're talking about now, Ms. Hollis. It is the transcript of the Tadic hearing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about the transcript that sets out the testimony of this witness in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Not a prior statement but prior sworn testimony given in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We object for the same reasons. We don't know on what basis he was cross-examined by counsel in the first case. The Defence strategy may have been quite different than any of the five here. Your Honours did not view this witness during his testimony in Tadic. You don't even know if the Trial Chamber in Tadic believed him or believed every word he said. So for that reason we object, on the same basis that we object to the prior statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the witness who has just finished his testimony, I think, or are we talking about the next witness? We're talking about the witness that is just coming in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Madam Hollis, are we talking about the witness that has just finished his testimony or the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about Edin Mrkalj, the witness we're calling now. That's why I raised the issue. It's not the statement of the prior witness, it is the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you. So the situation does not change, and I apologise for having to interrupt and for entering into it with this confusion. I haven't heard Mr. Fila, Mr. Tosic, and Mr. Jovan Simic yet. Mr. Fila, it is sufficient to have an objection to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am in favour of having Ms. Hollis's proposal adopted. So my opinion is different from the others, and that is why -- because the Tadic case is a public hearing. The transcript was public and was accessible to one and all. Therefore, I think that Madam Hollis is right, and my position differs from the others. But as I am alone in this opinion, then I don't think it will have much value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't feel I need to discuss the matter because we supported the position of Mr. Simic yesterday and Mr. O'Sullivan, so that we would like to wait and hear the Trial Chamber's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, to complete matters, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We join the opinion of Mr. O'Sullivan, our colleague, and we feel that at this moment we cannot go forward in that way. We do not feel that a decision can be made in the matter before a ruling is reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Hollis, as we have not had a ruling yet -- may I remind you that we will have to take into consideration the fact that there has been accord with regard to the parties relevant to the facts; that is to say, we still have not made our ruling, but we did say earlier on that the Trial Chamber does accept agreement with regard to fact. If that can assist you in any way in designing your examination-in-chief -- the Trial Chamber will not give you any instructions as to how you should do your work -- we just wish to remind you that the Appeals Chamber has no doubt with regard to the acceptance of generally recognised and acknowledged facts on which the parties have agreed, and I'd like to say that for the transcript. So Mr. Registrar, I think we can have the witness shown in at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me, Witness? Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration presented to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Would you please approach the microphone and make yourself comfortable. Can you hear me? Do you hear us properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for coming. You are now going to answer questions put to you by Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please state for the record your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: My name is Edin Mrkalj, and I was born on the 13th of June, 1965.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Biscani, the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you live in Biscani until you were 15 years old and then move to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you move back to the village of Biscani in January of 1988?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The village of Biscani, where is it located?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It is located in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How close is it to the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, the first houses are about three kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is the ethnic composition of the village, or what was the ethnic composition of the village of Biscani up until May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The village was populated exclusively with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could ask that Exhibit 1/26 be provided to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You, sir, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could take a moment to orient yourself to this map. And then if the portion of the map that shows the town of Prijedor could be placed on the overhead. If the witness could please point to Biscani on this map.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could we please have the technical people come in for a closer view of that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Biscani. As we are looking at this map, we see the area or the village of Rizvanovici. Are you familiar with that village?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then if we could move to the village of Carakovo, where is that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you also show us the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Also, if you could point to Rakovcani on the map.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this entire area that you have pointed to, what is this area known as? What is the term that is used to describe this area?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: This area was known as Brdo, or "hill."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This Brdo area, what was the ethnic composition of this area as of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was exclusively populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, up until the 10th of April of 1992, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was a policeman by profession, a security technician.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you train in Sarajevo at the School of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long was that training in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you study as part of this training?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was in the Internal Affairs school, and it was exclusively intended for the training of members of the public security services.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then did that train you to be an active-duty or regular police officer?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did that training you received include standards of conduct for police officers?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did it include police procedure and the structure of the Yugoslav police departments?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did it also include the command structure of the police?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the training also involve learning about duties and responsibilities of police officers and superiors?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What year did you complete your training?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was your first posting as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: In Belgrade, in the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What years did you work in Belgrade at the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I worked there until the 31st of December, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duties in Belgrade at the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Security for diplomatic and consular representative offices and buildings of vital state importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you say that your duties involved security for these offices and buildings, did that security include the security of personnel who worked in those buildings and offices?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As part of your ongoing responsibilities in this job, did you train to respond to different threat situations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As a result of your duties there and your training, did you have a heightened awareness of potential threat situations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated you worked for the federal SUP. What was the difference between the federal SUP and a republic-level SUP?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The difference was in territorial competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The republican SUP is active on the territory of a republic; the federal SUP has competence and authorisation to function in the whole area of the state, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then a local SUP, such as a SUP at Prijedor, what would be the competence of that SUP?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It would be territorial competence; that is to say, it would cover the territory covered by the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you returned to Biscani in January of 1988, what duties did you assume?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I worked in the public security service, public law and order, traffic and the criminal department, for crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what police department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The public security station of Prijedor. It was what we called the central Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At that time, how many police stations were in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There was the central police station in Prijedor; then there were local police stations that were situated in Ljubija, Kozarac, Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So there were four.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You worked in the Prijedor police station, the central station, until when?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I worked until April 1992. The 10th of April, 1992, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that you performed duties in public law and order, traffic, and the criminal department. When did you begin to work in the criminal department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was sometime in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your duties in the public law and order division and the traffic division, what were those duties?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I worked in an area, a region, as we referred to it, and my duty was to control all the important buildings and facilities, to work in the area of traffic control, to observe people who were interesting for our service, to maintain public law and order, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the position of "patrol sector leader"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did that position entail? What duties?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Individuals performing this duty had greater responsibility, because those individuals would be directly in charge of the region that this covered.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This would be a geographic region?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Within this region, how many villages could be included?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Depending on the region and how many villages, but usually five or six villages would comprise one region.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've said the person who had this person would be directly in charge of the region. What do you mean? Directly in charge in what ways? What duties would they have to perform?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Everything that happened in the area. All reports coming in, he'd have to deal with them. That person would be in charge of investigating matters, for example, on the basis of the reports. One of the functions would be, for instance, if a citizen wanted to have a permit issued for firearms, for example, then the number one man of that sector would make the decision whether that citizen could be granted a permit, whether he complied with all the stipulated conditions for carrying a firearm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was it typical that a patrol sector leader would have one or more subordinates?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, based on your training in Sarajevo and your experience as a police officer beginning in 1984, did the police in the former Yugoslavia have written rules or guidelines for proper procedure and conduct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How detailed were these guidelines or rules?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was very detailed and regulated the way in which the public security service was run.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kinds of police duties or procedures would be covered by these rules or guidelines?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The duties, rights, and obligations of the officer were specified in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This covered a variety of situations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did these guidelines also cover the responsibilities of superiors?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were regular or active-duty police officers required to be familiar with these duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were they required to be familiar with these rules and guidelines?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that was the right and duty of each and every one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you worked in the Prijedor Police Department, what was the ethnic composition of the Prijedor Police Department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: In Prijedor, there were Serb, Muslim, Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there any group that had a majority in the Prijedor Police Department?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992, beginning in January of 1992 up until you left the police department on the 10th of April of 1992, how would you characterise the relationship between non-Serbs and Serb police officers in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: That period -- did you say up until 1992? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. From January of 1992 until the 10th of April of 1992, when you left the Prijedor Police Department.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A lot had changed compared to the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What changes had you noticed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There were great changes in the behaviour of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of behaviour did you observe that had changed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, it wasn't what it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what way? Can you assist us in that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, some things that were in the air proved to be true. The relationships were not what they were before. These people had organised themselves far ahead of time; that is to say, they had their organisation. There were plans; plans existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who had their organisation? Who are you talking about by "these people" and "they"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I think this was organised by the people at the top, their top.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What group of people are you talking about? What ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In 1992, while you were still working for the Prijedor Police Department, who was the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if you know, after the Serb takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April, who was the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before you left the police, before the 10th of April of 1992, did you know a man by the name of Dzenadija who worked in the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his position in the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He had various functions. I think that at the end he was responsible for the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he a regular policeman, or did he hold a position of higher authority?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He held a higher position; he was one of the leaders, leading officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, why did you leave the police force?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Quite simply, everything was clear to me by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, the information that I had and what would be coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's 12.50. Do you wish to take a break at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Hollis. I think that the time has come for a very welcomed break. So let us have a half-hour break. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, you may continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as soon as that is possible. Please be seated. Now, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, before the break you were testifying about your leaving the Prijedor Police Department on the 10th of April of 1992. After you left the Prijedor Police Department, do you recall attending a police meeting in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, was this meeting held before or after the Serb takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: After the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who called this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The Serb Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The meeting was attended by somebody I didn't know, but he was introduced as a minister of the Serb Republic for Internal Affairs matters; then the president of the SDS, Simo Miskovic; then Commander Dule Jankovic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say Commander Dule Jankovic. Dule Jankovic was commander of what?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was commander of the public security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you know, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these people and yourself, who else attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Policemen of non-Serb ethnicity were invited to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this meeting? What was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I hear you saying what you're saying but I'm not getting the translation. Now I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. What was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The purpose of this meeting was the signing of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who had to sign loyalty?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What do you mean --

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What do you mean when they had to sign loyalty? What did they have to agree to be loyal to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: We were to have been loyal to the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was it explained to you what that would mean in terms of the duties you would have to perform?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: In the first place, it would mean that we would have to sign that loyalty, and by doing so we would belong to the Serb Republic. We would have to wear their insignia and markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was it explained to you what would happen if you did not sign this loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that if you did not sign the oath you would be able to continue your employment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I couldn't continue employment automatically, because they said who didn't sign employment would be terminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you sign that oath?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, on the 31st of May of 1992, were you given an order to turn in your police weapons the next day to the Prijedor Police Station?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you obey that order?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I had personal firearms, an automatic rifle, and a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So this was the 1st of June that you went to the Prijedor Police Station and surrendered your weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you allowed to leave the Prijedor Police Station once you had surrendered those weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No. No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened to you after you surrendered those weapons?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was searched immediately, the objects I had on me were seized, and I was taken upstairs to the crime department for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you held in the police department overnight?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the next day, were you taken to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, how were you transported to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: By bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there any other detainees on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No. I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there any other people on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The so-called interrogators and employees of the crime department from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The crime department from the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say "so-called interrogators," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Later I saw and learnt that these were people who were doing the interrogations in the Omarska camp, and that is why I used that term.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of these people?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken from Prijedor to Omarska, did you see anything unusual along the route?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: As we were driving, I was on the right-hand side, next to the window, and I noticed corpses placed in the form of a cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: These corpses placed in the form of a cross, did you observe injuries on their bodies?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, this was, for me, an eternity because I couldn't believe what I saw. But I could see well that the head was missing off one body and the head was attached to another body, and then there was an extra hand, and it was a horrific sight.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What clothing, if any, were these corpses wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What reaction, if any, did the interrogators have to these corpses along the road?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Everything was normal. I tried to bite my tongue but I thought to my myself, this is not possible. I was quite free to look left and right and in front of me. I didn't notice anything unusual on them, no change.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This area where you saw the corpses, if you know, what was the ethnic composition of that area?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The ethnic composition, the area was Serb, the area of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So this was at Omarska where you saw these corpses.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How close to the camp was it that you saw these corpses?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It's rather hard for me to tell. I can tell you very approximately. But it wasn't far; it was very close to the camp. Maybe 500 metres away or something like that. I can't be more precise because everything was horrific, and very soon after that we arrived at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, before you arrived at the camp, as you approached the camp, do you recall seeing a fire?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. On the left-hand side, as we were driving, so I turned to look the other way so as not to look at these bodies. I did see some fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw this fire, was there anything unusual or particular that you also noticed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There was a stench, the stench of human flesh. It was nauseating.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever smell such a stench while you were in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What circumstance was it that you smelled this similar stench?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A man whose hands were set on fire, Ferid Sikiric, and the smell was similar because the wounds were fresh. It's that same stench, the stench of human flesh.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know Ferid Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He's from the village of Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Until the camp was disbanded, which means the beginning of August. Until the last day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were detained at the Omarska camp, where were you held in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was held on the so-called pista, on the maintenance building, in the "white house." At night, sometimes, or rather quite frequently, we were taken to sleep in the canteen, so I was there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the maintenance building," was that also referred to as the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you spent at least some time in the "white house." How long were you in the "white house"? How many occasions?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I spent one night in the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What room were you in in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: When you go into the "white house," as far as I can recollect, the room was to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there other people in this room?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of the people you knew?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the condition of the room you were in?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was dreadful. There was blood; there was this stench. People were beaten up, in very bad shape. One person was covered with maggots on his body.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was a young man. After I learnt; at the time I didn't know what his name was. I know that Dr. Eso Hodzic undertook some surgery but with very primitive methods, he had no instruments; with a little knife, that's all he had.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This doctor that you mentioned, was he a detainee in the camp as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, he was detained in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Regarding the camp personnel, did you know any of those camp personnel before you were brought to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did you know from before?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I knew Miroslav Kvocka, Mladjo Radic, Zeljko Meakic, and almost all the investigators, the interrogators, the people who used to work with me in the same service.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Kvocka was a colleague of mine from work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I'd known him for a long time. He graduated a little earlier than me in Sarajevo, like me. We would see each other frequently at meetings, work meetings, so I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I knew Zeljko Meakic even better because we spent three years together in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Radic, how did you know Radic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Radic is also a colleague of ours; he is older than we are. But I knew him from work too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: For a long time. I met him in person when I arrived in Prijedor to take up employment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know him by any nickname?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was that nickname?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, on the 2nd of June, when you arrived at Omarska, where did you first go?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: For interrogation, to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What floor of the administration building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was the first floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did the interrogators go up to that first floor as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, they all went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see what room they went into?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you first were taken to the first floor of the administration building, were you held in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, they left me in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: About how long were you held in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was there from 10.00, 10.30, until I was taken in for interrogation. But it was quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this time you were in the hallway, what sounds, if any, did you hear coming from rooms up on this first floor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There were terrible screams uttered by people who were being taken in for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in the hallway, did you recognise anyone coming into the hallway?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did recognise some in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Miroslav Kvocka and Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: They were coming from the room into which the interrogators had entered when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, did you see them come into the hallway before, during, or after you heard these terrible sounds?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: They were there when the sounds were heard; they were in that room. They left the room; those screams continued, the beatings continued in the rooms, in the corridor. They passed through that way; they were present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did Miroslav Kvocka do when he came into the hallway?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He passed without -- ignoring me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He passed as if he never noticed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did Zeljko Meakic do?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He came up to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he explain to you why you were in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No. He just gave me a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: May I ask the witness be shown Exhibit 3/77B, that is, the diagram of the first floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you please look at that diagram, and then would you please use the pointer and would you show the Judges the hallway that you were in when you were taken up to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You're moving your pointer along B8; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, would you show the Judges the room into which the interrogators went.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The largest room on the left; it is the room marked B1.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you point to the room from which Zeljko Meakic and Miroslav Kvocka came.

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You're also pointing to B1; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. They came out of that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could retrieve the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that for a period of time while you were in Omarska you stayed on the pista. How long did you stay on the pista?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Roughly 60 days -- no, sorry, 40 days. About 40 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were on the pista, how often, if ever, did you see Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I saw him several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw him, where would he be?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I would see him entering or coming out of the administration building or when the shifts were changing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see him during the day and the night?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw him in the camp, what would he wear?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The so-called camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform of whom? Of the police or of the military?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It is the police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you describe that uniform for us?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It's a uniform which differs from normal uniforms which are in one colour. The camouflage uniform has sort of spots on it in different colours; two colours: light blue and dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have marked an exhibit, it was previously marked 3/22, and we would ask that it be shown to the witness. Would you please first show it to Defence counsel. First show it to Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, would you look at this photograph. Look at that uniform, please, and then if the uniform could be put on the overhead. What is this uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: That is the uniform we are talking about, that he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you saw Kvocka in the camp, what weapons did he have?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He had a rifle on him, the so-called pump-action, Pumperica, gun, which he carried like this, in his right hand; and he also had a glove without fingers. You could recognise him by the way he carried this rifle; that is, the people who didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, what was your understanding of his position in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was the first commander of the Omarska camp. The commander, the man who ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why did you conclude that he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: By what I saw, by what I heard, and the third reason, the person who told me everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This person who told you everything, what was his position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: That person had the function of some sort of external security guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he tell you about Kvocka's position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: That he was the number one man.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said you also concluded that from what you saw. What did you see to lead you to conclude that he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: When shifts were changing, then he would frequently be present, and the shift leaders would be with him and they would address him, and from that I could conclude that he was, indeed, what they said. Also, I wasn't present, but he introduced himself personally as the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this is what you heard from other detainees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that from other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Kvocka present when detainees were abused or called out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often did you see him present when detainees were abused?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about those incidents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, on one occasion, we were on the pista and he was in front of the administration building. This was during the daytime; I can't remember the time exactly but it was daylight. He was with a number of those guards, standing together in front of the administration building. Then suddenly the order came that we had to lie down; the word used was "Zelijezi," which meant lie down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after you were ordered to lie down?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: We did. People were not in their proper places, some, and they looked for some room, and I laid down and immediately they came and started beating a man who was lying next to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know this man?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that man personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was an engineer, Ilijaz Drobic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened to Drobic as a result of the beating he received?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was killed. He was killed there and left there to lie amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there anyone else close to you who was beaten during this incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. Lower down from me a man was lying, I don't remember his surname. I know his first name and where he was from.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The man is from the village of Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know what injuries, if any, he suffered as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was killed by the beating, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, how soon after you saw Kvocka by the administration building, how soon after that did these beatings begin?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Immediately. He was there. We were allowed to look left and right. There were no orders, and then suddenly the order came. Suddenly. We didn't hear it straight away, and then it was repeated and we threw ourselves to the ground. We had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said you saw him present on several occasions when people were abused or taken out. You've indicated one such occasion. What other occasions was he present when people were abused or taken out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was present when they brought people to the camp, we could see that from the pista, because when these people would get off the vehicle, they would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was he present on any occasion when a person was called out and did not return?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was this person who was called out and didn't return?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was Izet Memic. He had a nickname, Puco.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened when he was called out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: When he was called out, Kvocka came with Meakic and another guard, they came to fetch him. The guard called him out and the man got up and went off, and as he was in the group where I was, he did not return. We waited for him to return. This was just before the shift, the evening shift. I can't tell you the exact time but it was in the evening. And the second shift to take over, which would be taking on the night shift, it came to look for him, and then someone said that he had been taken off. There was a man who worked on the maintenance of Omarska, and he came about an hour later -- it was about 8.00 in the evening; he would always come around that time -- and we told him, that is to say, I personally said to him, "Puco is not here. He's gone off." And then he said, "Well, just so long as you're alive and well."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he say what had happened to Puco?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was this person who told you that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was one of the inmates of the camp, Midho Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also indicated that you knew Radic prior to coming to the camp. While you were on the pista, how often, if ever, did you see Radic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Very often, because he was the man in charge of shift number 3, as it was called. That means he spent 12 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you would see him, what would he be doing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was the head of that shift. It was what we called shift number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why do you say that he was the head of that shift?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was the leader of the shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see or hear to make you conclude that he was the leader of that shift?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: First of all, it was the worst shift in the camp. A crime is a crime, but it was worst when his shift was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your statement that he was the leader of the shift. I'd like you to tell the Judges what you saw or heard that led you to believe he was the leader of that shift?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Everybody knew that; we all knew it. The man working in security confirmed that, he said, "Yes, he is the leader. He is the leader of that shift."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there anything about his behaviour or the behaviour of others toward him that led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He would come with his shift; he would talk to the commander when the shifts were changing. Then he had a room upstairs somewhere in the administration building as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did he wear when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He wore a normal -- a standard police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What weapons, if any, would he have?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Radic present when detainees were either beaten or called out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often would you see him present when detainees were beaten?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, when they were brought in, when they brought the people there, or when they took people off for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often was he present when you saw people called out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did all of these people return who were called out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The ones who did return, what was their condition when they returned?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: They were in a very serious condition, very bad condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were detained at Omarska, did you ever encounter a person by the name of Prcac?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was this a person you knew before coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, but not very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know him before you came to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He worked -- that is to say, before, he was a colleague of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when did you first see him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: When he came and when he was the so-called third commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you first saw him, where were you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: We were on the pista. I was on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you being held on the pista at that time or were you merely on the pista for that day?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: We were already in the hangar, but there were days when they would take us out again to the pista.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw him that day, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I saw him that day; he had some documents that he was carrying. And there were several of their people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: An army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was it a regular army uniform from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I saw him that first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you saw him and he was carrying these documents, where did he go?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was going in the direction of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often after that did you see him in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Several times, a couple of times, and afterwards when there was the roll-call and when the camp was disbanded. He was there for a very short time so that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when there was the roll-call when the camp was disbanded, you said you saw Prcac at that time. What was he doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There was a roll-call; he was calling out the names of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What weapons, if any, did he have when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that Krkan was the shift leader for the third shift. How many shifts of guards were there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There were three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Other than Krkan, did you know any of the shift leaders before you came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in the camp, did you learn the names of any of these shift leaders?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were the names of the shift leaders?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: One was called Milojica Kos; I didn't know him. Then there was that other one, Ckalja, Gruban, something like that; I didn't know him before either.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You talked a bit about Prcac. You said you didn't see him very often. Was he ever present when people were abused or called out?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to the 16th of June, while you were in Omarska. On that date, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift was on duty when you were beaten on that date?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I think it was shift number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Whose shift was that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Mladjo Radic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who beat you on the 16th of June?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know Dusko Tadic before you were brought to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic work at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He came to Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What time of the day was it when this beating occurred?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was during the daytime, at about 2.00, 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did this beating occur?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: In the administration building, on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: That day was our first official registration day, that is to say, for the detainees. I was standing in a group of 30 people who were on the list, and someone unknown to me called me out and another minor, and we were sent to take out somebody from the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This person you were sent to take out, what was their condition?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: In a very bad condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened when you went to get this person?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The person, that is, the minor standing next to me was hit and he fell down, and when he came to they sent him back, and then I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I went upstairs and it was my turn. I was beaten. A pipe was put in my mouth. I was hit with a metal bar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was doing this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: After that, when I fell down and when I regained consciousness, I was ordered -- he ordered me to hit the person lying down. When we came in, the person was already on the ground. I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the condition of this person that you were forced to hit?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He was in a catastrophic state. It's very difficult to explain. A dreadful state.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What part of his body did you hit him on?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The head.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the condition of his head when you hit him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I couldn't recognise him, whether it was a man or what it was. It was all smashed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you hit him, what did it feel like?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There was a groan, a cry. The man was still giving out signs of life. It is very difficult to describe the sounds that came from him, and the whole thing. But I had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened --

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was forced to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened after you hit him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was ordered to go back downstairs, from where I'd come.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you said that this beating occurred on the first floor of the restaurant building. Where was it on the first floor? Was it in one of the rooms or was it in the hallway?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What injuries did you suffer as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I had very serious injuries. When my wounds cooled down, I couldn't actually keep my head up. Two people had to carry me, I wasn't able to walk, and one of them had to hold my head up. And that's how it was for the first three days afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What parts of your body were injured as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: My hand and my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you suffer any injuries to your teeth as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When I say "my head," I mean my teeth as well. They were all -- some of them had been -- I'd lost some of them, and the teeth that remained were pushed back into my gums.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever given any medical care for these injuries?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there any other occasions at the camp when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did these beatings occur?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Particularly during a visit to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: A visit by whom?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: There was a lot of security about then. We were all lined up in rows, we had to sing songs, and after that, we were ordered to go into the kitchen, the canteen, allegedly to go and have some food. At the entrance, in the hallway, they were waiting for us with batons and metal rods and began to beat us. And they had spilt some liquid on the floor, so they made you run and then you would slip and fall over, and this would continue and other people would slip in turn and fall over you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say "they were waiting." Who was waiting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The time that you were beaten, did any camp personnel ever intervene to stop those beatings?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier about the existence of very detailed rules and guidelines that govern police behaviour. Did those rules and guidelines govern how prisoners were to be treated by the police?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If, as a policeman, you had to provide security to prisoners in a gaol or a prison, what duties would you have with regard to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, there are precise, specific rules and regulations governing conduct, your conduct towards prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would that conduct have to include?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A prisoner also has his rights. The individual has the right to medical assistance, to be given food; they have the right to use the toilet facilities, and all the other rights that prisoners enjoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who's responsible to ensure that those prisoners get those rights?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The leading officer, in keeping with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As to each individual police officer, do they have a duty to provide those rights to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What duties, if any, of protection of these prisoners do police officers have?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The rules and regulations specify our behaviour towards prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would be your duties to protect prisoners?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I would have to ensure their safety and security, of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if valuables were taken from prisoners, such as money or other valuables, what duties, under the rules and regulations you have talked about, what duties would the police have regarding those valuables?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: A report would be made of the items taken and they would be submitted in three copies which would be signed. The authorising official taking away this property would sign the paper and the person whose property was being taken away would also sign a copy, and one copy would be given to the prisoner and the others would be placed in the archives for the purposes of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Regarding the valuables themselves, would they be held for that prisoner?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because they are his personal property.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, under the rules and the guidelines you worked under, what responsibility or what consequence would there be if a police officer violated these duties?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Once again, the rules and regulations stipulate what happens. He would have to suffer the consequences if his conduct was in opposition to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, as a police officer, if you saw another police officer committing a crime, what would be your obligation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It is the right and duty to prevent an individual from performing anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: This would be true even if the perpetrator were a police officer?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, because the rules hold true for policemen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you were the superior of police officers and you became aware that your subordinates were committing crimes, what would be your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, the rules also regulate what is to be done in such cases. That individual would lose his job automatically, and of course this depended on the crime that he had committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, would the superior have the authority to suspend this person or relieve them of duties pending an investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that would be automatic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were policemen allowed to drink while they were performing duty?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If other police officers saw a policeman drinking on duty, what would be their duties, what would be their obligation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: He would have to report him to his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would a superior be allowed to provide alcohol to policemen who were on duty?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in regard to providing security to gaols or prisons and to prisoners, what rules, if any, existed about the use of firearms?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Well, the rules and regulations provide for this, and the use of firearms is specified as well. Once again, there are conditions under which the authorised personnel may use firearms; this would be stipulated, where and when this is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Under what conditions would you be able to shoot a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Once again, there are the rules and regulations governing the use of firearms when prisoners are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Under what kind of general circumstances would you be allowed to shoot a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: If the individual -- that is to say, the authorised individual is duty-bound to use firearms to prevent the execution of a crime and to refute an attack; that is to say, if somebody else's life is in danger, the life of another citizen or his own life, then he may resort to the use of firearms.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If a prisoner was ordered to sit down and a prisoner refused to do so and stood up and moved forward and this prisoner were unarmed, based on your training and experience and the guidelines you worked under, would the police be able to shoot this prisoner?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No. No, there would be no grounds for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If a superior were present at the time, what would be the superior's duties?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: If the superior were present and something like that took place, he would have to prevent it. But if the superior, according to the rules which specify this, that is to say, if the superior aids and abets a crime to take place, then he is equally responsible for the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if the superior were not present but the superior learned about this incident, what would be the superior's responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Once again, the rules specify this. If there is the doubt that somebody -- the suspicion that somebody has committed a crime, then it is the superior's duty to bring an investigation against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you were in the camp from the 2nd of June until the beginning of August. Based on what you observed and what happened to you, was the behaviour of the police officers in the Omarska camp consistent with the rules and guidelines you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about people you identified as having positions of superior authority in the camp. Based on your training and your experience and these guidelines you talked about, the behaviour of these superiors that you observed, was that in accordance with the rules and guidelines?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about this visit to the camp. Do you know who it was who was visiting the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was it who was visiting the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: It was a politician, Vojo Kupresanin from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you observe anything to indicate to you that there were representatives from the federal government as well?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you observe to lead you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The number plates on the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was significant about the numbers on the plates?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: The number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Vehicles belonging to the federal SUP had number plates beginning with a 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, when you left Omarska, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: We were taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Until the camp was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you go from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: We went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your physical condition when you were taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: I was in good physical condition when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you left Omarska, how would you describe your physical condition?

utterances.speaker: EDIN MRKALJ
utterances.text: Extremely poor. I was seriously ill because of everything that I had experienced there, and I was given no assistance. I lost a lot of weight. And generally my condition was very, very poor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
